title: Clarinet harmony, 'Dixieland' as a label and Bunk's complaints about his band
summary: Clarinet harmony versus independent parts, Bunk's remark on ragtime, jazz and swing, and his friction with Jim Robinson and George Lewis in New York.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Al Rose was telling me that when he grew up listening in the bands that the clarinet and the trumpet always were in harmony together, and the clarinet was not a counterpoint to the trumpet, but he rarely hears that now, that Harry Shields was the last one he knew of that actually harmonized with the trumpet player.

Yeah, occasionally some of the other musicians do it today, but to me, I never heard music here before, say 1930, 38 maybe, it was the first time I ever heard any music here. And so all we have to do, go by, are the old records. But to me, that's been more, to me, a more later development. Some people try to make a big difference between the terms like Dixieland and traditional New Orleans jazz and all, which is mainly just words in people's minds. Because like Bunk once said, we always called it ragtime, and from ragtime we went to jazz, and then we went to swing, and now we're going back to ragtime.
I don't remember any clarinet play I was playing or harmony part down here on the early records.
I never heard of a single one. I would say if you're going to make it a very loose unison sometimes is about all.

The places I've heard it mostly has been later bands and mostly some of the white so-called Dixieland type bands where they harmonize together. To me, it isn't an interesting style. I mean, it's getting into the arranged, well, one of a better word, say, the Sousa march style or something else or any other written out popular tunes where you just write it all out in harmony because that's the big feature of the New Orleans, the independence of all those parts. In the early records I made, sometimes Bunk and Jim Robinson would play a good deal together, but that's because, not to criticize them, that if Jim didn't know the tune he'd sometimes stick to the melody a good deal if he didn't know the tune or the harmony and hardly knew the tune he'd try to follow the melody along, but that used to worry Bunk a lot. Bunk used to complain bitterly to me about that. That was one of his criticisms of Jim. As I say, they had a lot of friction in the band in New York finally, even with George Lewis and the different ones that Bunk would make a statement calling them emergency musicians, they weren't that bad of course, they did some wonderful playing. George and Jim and all of them. But it wasn't the type of band that Bunk had wanted exactly. He would rather have had somebody that could read so they could pick up new popular tunes and learn them in a hurry so they could either play requests or if they'd had any radio jobs the radio job might tell them to play a tune for say one minute and 41 seconds they have there to do that. And you start a New Orleans band playing the chorus of a tune several times and you don't know how long it's going to come out. It's pretty hard to regulate it. So I mean that's an example of the criticism that Bunk had of people. One thing he objected to is if the trombone did try to follow him too closely and say the same rhythm part and especially when Jim would almost double on the melody in Octaflower which really I might say bugged him to death.
